newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says World Bank report balanced.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says World Bank report balanced.

text.p: Indonesian Planning Minister Ginanjar Kartasasmita said on Friday the World Bank's recent report on Indonesia was balanced.
"The report is balanced in general. Some of the points are encouraging," Ginanjar told reporters.
He, however, added that there were suggestions that were not in line with government policies.
"There are suggestions we can use but also there are some which we can't. We could follow some of the advice but it will depend on the timing," he said.
The World Bank said in its 1997 report on Indonesia that the country should have fiscal measures ready to cope with possible overheating of the economy.
The bank suggested Indonesia take some fast-acting measures, including raising taxes on urban properties and raising domestic fuel prices to eliminate subsidies in the budget.

Other stand-by measures it recommended included raising power tariffs, cutting down tax exemptions, increasing forestry royalties, making more goods subject to luxury taxes and bringing more off-budget spending into the budget.
Darmoko Slamet, secretary general of the mining and energy ministry, was quoted by the afternoon daily Suara Pembangunan as saying the bank's recommendation on fuels was inappropriate.
Slamet said fuel subsidies were needed especially for those consumed by the vast majority of the population.
"Major fuels are no longer subsidied. Now (there are subsidies) only on kerosene and diesel fuel, which are widely used," he said.
Slamet said subsidies were still needed to support the country's economic growth, but they will be abolished in phases.
Economists were worried over the immediate implications on fuel prices if the government followed the bank's suggestion.
They said a cut in fuel subsidies would boost prices and spur inflation, which had been well contained recently, with further reductions expected.

Saleh Afiff, co-ordinating minister for economics and finance, said the bank had made similar recommendations in its report last year but they were not implemented by the government because of their widespread implications.
Afiff said Indonesia's current account deficit was still manageable although it was showing a widening trend.
The bank said Indonesia's current account deficit was likely to reach $10.1 billion, or four percent of GDP, in the fiscal 1997/98 year (April-March) from $8.823 billion in 1996/97.
Afiff said Indonesia's economic fundamentals remained healthy and the current account deficit was within an acceptable level.
